headline: Match the frequency of every letter
statement: Determine whether t is an anagram of s: t must contain exactly the same characters with exactly the same multiplicities, in any order.
constraints: Both strings contain lowercase English letters
intuition: Order changes under an anagram, but counts do not. First reject different lengths, then consume each t character from a count of s. A negative count identifies a character used too often.
approach: Count each character of s in counts.
Consume each t character, rejecting a deficit; if no deficit occurs, equal length guarantees all counts balance.
correctness: Equal multisets are necessary for rearrangement and sufficient because each t character can be matched to a distinct corresponding s character. Consuming without deficits uses all available copies, and equal lengths ensure none are left over.
bruteForce: Sort both strings and compare the sorted sequences, costing O(n log n) time.

complexity.explanation: Only a count per lowercase letter is stored.

pitfalls: Presence alone is insufficient: multiplicity matters.
The reference can count arbitrary Unicode code points if the domain is extended, but visually identical text may require Unicode normalization first.
